hops.title: Cold fingers go clumsy but keep stinging
hops.text: On a cold morning your fingers fumble a zipper and go dull to light touch, while the cold itself keeps stinging. Cooling an excitable membrane progressively deepens the voltage-dependent slow inactivation of tetrodotoxin-sensitive sodium channels, so fewer are left available to open. In rodent recordings, Nav1.8 resisted that cold-induced shift in steady-state slow inactivation; though cooling slows its kinetics and lowers peak current, it could still supply current to keep some nociceptive endings firing in cooled skin. Mice lacking Nav1.8 showed negligible foot lifting and jumping on a 0 °C plate, whereas later work found unchanged transient responses in above-freezing assays, including 5 and 10 °C plates.

sources.citation: Zimmermann K, Leffler A, Babes A, et al. Sensory neuron sodium channel Nav1.8 is essential for pain at low temperatures. Nature 447:855-858 (2007), PMID 17568746.
Luiz AP, MacDonald DI, Santana-Varela S, et al. Cold sensing by NaV1.8-positive and NaV1.8-negative sensory neurons. Proc Natl Acad Sci USA 116:3811-3816 (2019), PMID 30755524.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Bare hands fumbling with a winter coat zipper on a frosty morning, with knit mittens tucked under one arm.
image.caption: In some cooled rodent nociceptors, fewer tetrodotoxin-sensitive channels remain available while Nav1.8 helps sustain firing.

hops.title: The show-horse line that inherited periodic paralysis
hops.text: Quarter Horse judges once prized a heavily muscled stallion named Impressive, and selective breeding spread his line fast. It also spread hyperkalemic periodic paralysis, traced in 1992 to a single phenylalanine-to-leucine swap in the adult skeletal-muscle sodium channel; affected horses tend to be the heavily muscled ones judges rewarded. Cell-attached recordings found the defect was impaired inactivation: bursts of persistent current, with an open probability about eight times control at the end of a 40-millisecond pulse. During an attack, elevated potassium and that persistent current can hold fibres depolarized, and if enough normal channels inactivate, a fibre temporarily cannot fire.

sources.citation: Naylor JM. Hyperkalemic periodic paralysis. Vet Clin North Am Equine Pract 13:129-144 (1997), PMID 9106348.
Rudolph JA, Spier SJ, Byrns G, et al. Periodic paralysis in quarter horses: a sodium channel mutation disseminated by selective breeding. Nat Genet 2:144-147 (1992), PMID 1338908.
Cannon SC, Hayward LJ, Beech J, Brown RH Jr. Sodium channel inactivation is impaired in equine hyperkalemic periodic paralysis. J Neurophysiol 73:1892-1899 (1995), PMID 7623088.
Cannon SC, Brown RH Jr, Corey DP. A sodium channel defect in hyperkalemic periodic paralysis: potassium-induced failure of inactivation. Neuron 6:619-626 (1991), PMID 1849724.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A heavily muscled chestnut Quarter Horse standing calmly in a sunlit wooden barn beside a plain blue ribbon.
image.caption: Persistent sodium current and high potassium can depolarize muscle fibres enough to inactivate the channels firing needs.

hops.afterHeading: Blocking Nav1.8: from a fitted curve to a spike
hops.title: A mouse that uses its prey's venom as a Nav1.8 blocker
hops.text: Southern grasshopper mice hunt and eat Arizona bark scorpions, whose venom increased firing in isolated house-mouse sensory neurons. A stung grasshopper mouse grooms the spot briefly and finishes the meal. Its Nav1.8 carries amino-acid variants linked to venom-dependent inhibition of sodium current and reduced or blocked firing in isolated sensory neurons, which the authors interpret as toxin binding that blocks spike propagation. Rowe and colleagues note that losing pain in general is rare and risky, since pain reports damage; in this mouse, whole venom instead inhibits Nav1.8-dependent signalling rather than exciting sensory neurons.

sources.citation: Rowe AH, Xiao Y, Rowe MP, Cummins TR, Zakon HH. Voltage-gated sodium channel in grasshopper mice defends against bark scorpion toxin. Science 342:441-446 (2013), PMID 24159039.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A small sandy-brown grasshopper mouse standing on moonlit desert sand facing a bark scorpion near a cactus.
image.caption: Arizona bark scorpion venom inhibited Nav1.8 current and reduced firing in isolated sensory neurons from southern grasshopper mice.
